questions.question: A patient who has previously undergone a transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) presents with fever, new-onset dyspnea, and worsening heart failure. What are the primary diagnostic steps and imaging modalities required to distinguish between structural valve deterioration and prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE)?

In the context of prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE), current guidelines generally favor surgical valve replacement over transcatheter interventions. In a patient with high surgical risk and multiple prior TAVIs, what specific clinical and anatomical criteria must be met to justify a transcatheter-in-transcatheter (TAV-in-TAV) approach instead of surgery?

During a TAV-in-TAV procedure, the 'neo-skirt' refers to the accumulation of displaced leaflets and thrombus/debris beneath the new valve frame. How does the strategy of 'high implantation' help mitigate the risks associated with the neo-skirt, specifically regarding coronary artery perfusion and effective orifice area?
When planning a repeat TAVI (TAV-in-TAV or TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV), which specific parameters on multislice CT (MSCT) are critical to assess to prevent iatrogenic coronary artery obstruction?

Following the third TAVI in this case, the patient initially exhibited a high mean gradient (67 mmHg) and a low indexed aortic valve area (0.4 cm²/m²), suggesting severe patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM), yet these parameters improved significantly after one month. What physiological or technical factors can explain this early post-procedural hemodynamic evolution?
Why is commissural alignment prioritized during a repeat TAVI procedure, and how does this impact the long-term lifetime management of the patient's coronary arteries?
